output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Jake Thompson (22) works as a certified nursing assistant (CNA) in a memory care unit. He is known as Jake. His scrubs are slightly wrinkled, sneakers gray from linoleum, bags under his eyes make him look older. He is restless: drums fingers, taps foot, has applied for travel nursing contracts in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Nome; brochures in locker. He tells himself Alaska is about wilderness and challenge, but also about distance from the unit, his parents' disappointment, and the business school he left after one semester. His father (mechanical engineer) still expects him to return to degree; his mother (nurse practitioner) suggested CNA training and hopes he settles. He grew up in suburban Indianapolis, middle class, with a culture of practical achievement (degree, job, house). His values are a tangle of that pragmatism and a belief that meaning comes from showing up for people who are falling apart. He hates feeling hollow after a resident's death but hates the idea of doing anything else. There is a tension between wanting to stay and wanting to run. His personal history includes a night in sophomore year when he felt revulsion during a marketing project, closed his laptop, called his mother at 2 a.m. crying, and she drove three hours to pick him up. That shame of needing rescue and relief of being taken away shapes his decision-making; he wants to be the one who rescues. He knows the night shift CNA: she always says thank you, once brought him a bagel after he covered, has a young daughter, often needs last-minute coverage (he provided twice). He feels a mild unspoken obligation because she once saved him from a difficult situation when he forgot his badge. His tendency is to say yes to coverage requests; in the past three months he said yes to every shift trade unless he had a prior commitment. He often tells himself he will say no next time but when the moment comes he imagines the other person's relief and agrees. He holds the value that meaning comes from showing up for people falling apart and being the rescuer. He has completed CNA training and developed skill in managing residents' stimulation through music and routine. He does not have a college degree.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Jake arrives at the memory care unit fifteen minutes before his shift starts. The break room is empty except for a half-full pot of coffee and a note from the night shift CNA asking if anyone can cover the last hour of her shift tomorrow. He could sit down, drink his coffee, and mentally prepare for the day, or he could respond to the note and offer to help, knowing it will mean another long day. The choice is his.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Jake has already worked five doubles this month. His body aches, especially his lower back and the balls of his feet. He is emotionally flat, not dreading the day but not energized. He has a small constant headache from poor sleep and too much caffeine. The note's handwriting reminds him of a similar request two weeks ago that led to an exhausting thirteen-hour day. He sees the half-empty coffee pot and recalls the night he called his mother at 2 a.m., her voice steady as she said she would be there soon.
